definition: The growth function, also called the shatter coefficient or the shattering number, measures the richness of a set family or class of functions.
details: It is especially used in the context of statistical learning theory, where it is used to study properties of statistical learning methods. The term 'growth function' was coined by Vapnik and Chervonenkis in their 1968 paper, where they also proved many of its properties. It is a basic concept in machine learning.

explainer.lead: The growth function counts how many different ways a class of functions can label a set of points, taking the maximum over all choices of points. It gives a precise way to describe the richness of that class and is used to study statistical learning methods.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a box of rules for sorting dots into two groups, such as red and blue. The growth function asks how many different color patterns the rules can make on a given number of dots, using the arrangement of dots that allows the most patterns.
tiers.practitioner: Use the growth function when analyzing the expressiveness of a function class rather than when training a particular model. For each sample size n, consider every placement of n points and count the distinct binary labelings the class can produce, then take the maximum. A common pitfall is treating this worst-case combinatorial count as a guarantee about performance on a particular dataset.
tiers.paperLevel: For a class H of binary functions, the growth function is Pi_H(n) = max over x_1,...,x_n of |{(h(x_1),...,h(x_n)) : h in H}|. Vapnik and Chervonenkis coined the term in their 1968 paper and proved many of its properties. Because the definition maximizes over point configurations, it summarizes worst-case richness rather than behavior on one fixed sample.

explainer.example: Suppose a class contains only two functions: one labels every point positive and the other labels every point negative. On any three points, it produces only +++ and ---, so its growth function at n = 3 is 2.

usedIn.name: Machine learning research
usedIn.detail: Used as a basic concept for analyzing classes of functions.

explainer.intuition: A richer class can produce more distinct label patterns as the number of points grows. The growth function tracks the largest possible pattern count at each sample size.
howItWorks: Choose a class of binary functions.
Fix a number n of points.
Count the distinct label patterns the class can produce on a point configuration.
Maximize that count over all configurations of n points.
Repeat for other values of n.
explainer.whyItMatters: It turns the vague idea of a function class being more or less expressive into a count that can be analyzed. This makes it useful for studying statistical learning methods.
misconceptions: It is not simply the number of functions in the class.
It is a maximum over point configurations, not a count for one fixed sample.
Greater richness alone does not guarantee better learning performance.
